ideas.title: How you drive, not how fast, flagged coming cognitive decline about 18 months before diagnosis in a small WashU study
ideas.angle: GPS trackers in older drivers' cars picked up changes in cornering and in how many different places people drove. Those changes came before a mild cognitive impairment diagnosis by a median of 18 months, with no gene or memory test needed. The useful idea for readers is that losing your 'range' (going to fewer places) may be an early sign worth noticing. The caveat fits in a clause: only 25 people actually declined.
ideas.why_now: Online 7 days ago (date verified) and not widely covered. Passive tracking and wearables for early dementia detection is a live consumer-tech topic.
ideas.is_it_real: It's an early signal, not a test. 298 older adults were followed, but only 25 progressed to impairment, all at a single center. The prediction accuracy (AUC 0.75) is moderate: useful in research, nowhere near diagnostic. It links driving changes to decline and doesn't show cause. The tie to the blood marker pTau217 was only 'directional'. The same WashU driving project has been covered before, which is why this is a roundup item and not a pitch. Say 'linked to' or 'flagged', never 'predicts Alzheimer's'.

studies.journal: The Journals of Gerontology: Series B
studies.headline: How you drive — not how fast — may predict Alzheimer's up to 18 months before diagnosis
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 progressors — only 25 converters), single-center, short follow-up relative to disease timeline

ideas.title: Baking soda with a carb-heavy breakfast cut about 30 seconds off recreational women's 10K times, with no extra stomach trouble
ideas.angle: This is one of the rare sports-supplement trials run on recreational women runners instead of male athletes. Baking soda is an old trick that usually causes gut distress, but taken with a carb-rich meal 90 minutes before the run it gave about a 1% gain (32 seconds over roughly 51 minutes). Stomach symptoms were no worse than with placebo. The caveat: the dose is not 'a spoonful'.
ideas.why_now: Online 3 days ago (date verified). It fits the running thread of 'sports science is finally studying women', and fall race season is under way.
ideas.is_it_real: It's a properly run double-blind, randomized crossover trial, but small (21 women, one center in Türkiye, one race each way). The time gain was statistically significant but modest. The digest's 'spoonful' framing is wrong. The dose was 0.3 g per kg of body weight, several teaspoons for most women. By my own arithmetic (not from the paper), that is roughly 5 g of sodium for a 60 kg runner, about double the recommended daily limit. That matters for anyone with high blood pressure, and the item should say so. No one should try it for the first time on race day.

studies.journal: International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
studies.headline: Baking soda taken with a carb-heavy meal shaves time off a 10-km race for recreational female runners — with almost no stomach trouble
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, short follow-up, study population from Türkiye

ideas.title: Spinal cord injury deaths have climbed since 2016 among Americans 55 to 74, and falls drive most of them in the oldest
ideas.angle: In 25 years of US death certificates, spinal cord injury deaths fell among young adults while they rose 43% to 60% among people 55 to 74 after 2016. Falls account for 59% of these deaths in people 85 and older. For readers, it's another number arguing for strength and balance work in midlife, not just in old age.
ideas.why_now: Online 3 days ago (date verified). With winter coming and ice-related falls ahead, it's a timely reason to bring up fall prevention.
ideas.is_it_real: The data are real and national (31,279 deaths from CDC WONDER). But this is ecological death-certificate data with no individual detail. It can't say why deaths rose, and changes in how deaths are coded could be part of it. Before the item runs, check whether the 43–60% rise is in age-specific rates or raw counts, since an aging population alone would raise counts. The reported disparities (men 3.59 times the rate of women, Black adults 1.75 times that of white adults) are rate ratios and should be described that way, not as 'times more likely'. Fall prevention already has two routed pitches, so this belongs as a short item, not a new pitch.

studies.journal: The Journal of Spinal Cord Medicine
studies.headline: Spinal Cord Injury Deaths Are Rising Fast in Older Americans — and Falls Are the Biggest Driver
studies.caveats: observational design, ecological study (CDC WONDER death records), no individual-level data
